meaning: Rendering is computing the image that a camera would see of a scene that exists only as numbers in a simulator.
A physics engine is the software that moves a simulated scene forward in time. PhysX, Newton and MuJoCo Warp are the physics engines in this section.
A mesh is a surface stored as a set of triangles. A simulator stores every shape it draws as a mesh.
Rasterisation makes an image by projecting each triangle onto it and filling the pixels that the triangle covers.
Ray tracing makes an image by following a ray from the camera through each pixel to the surface it hits, and then sending more rays from that point.
A shadow ray is a ray sent from a point on a surface toward a light. If something blocks it, the point is in shadow.
A BVH is a tree of nested boxes around the triangles of a scene. A ray tracer walks down this tree to find the first triangle that a ray hits.
RT cores are a hardware unit on some NVIDIA GPUs that speeds up the BVH walk, the most expensive step of ray tracing. Data-centre training GPUs such as the H100 do not have them.
Tensor cores are the units of an NVIDIA GPU that multiply matrices. Matrix multiplication is the arithmetic that training and running a neural network rely on.

The general compute cores are the units of a GPU that run ordinary GPU code. They run batched physics, ray tracers written as GPU code, the parts of a neural network other than its matrix multiplications, and the lighting and shading of an RTX renderer.
NVENC is the fixed-function engine on an NVIDIA GPU that compresses frames into video.
NVDEC is the fixed-function engine on an NVIDIA GPU that turns video back into frames.
AV1 is the video codec that LeRobot writes by default. Some data-centre GPUs cannot decode it in hardware.
RTX rendering is NVIDIA's name for rendering that hands the search for what each ray hits to the RT cores. Isaac Sim's renderer works this way.
A headless run is a simulation with no camera images and no interactive view. Isaac Lab 3.0's installation guide adds a renderer's requirements only when you need one of the two.
An environment is one simulated copy of the scene together with its task. Training runs thousands of environments side by side on one GPU.
Cartpole is a small standard control task in which a cart balances a pole. Isaac Lab uses it in its benchmark.
Tiled rendering draws the camera of every environment into its own tile of one large GPU image in a single pass. The image is then cut into a tensor that the policy reads directly in GPU memory.
Isaac Sim is NVIDIA's simulator application. It renders with RTX and requires a GPU with RT cores.
Isaac Lab is NVIDIA's robot-learning framework. Since version 3.0, it can run without Isaac Sim.
G and P are EC2 GPU instance families. G instances have GPUs with RT cores, and P instances have data-centre training GPUs.
Direct lighting is light that reaches a surface straight from a lamp, without bouncing off other surfaces. Isaac Lab's Newton Warp renderer computes only direct lighting.
Warp is NVIDIA's framework for writing GPU code in Python. MuJoCo Warp and the Newton Warp renderer are built on it.
OVRTX is the RTX renderer that Isaac Lab 3.0's documentation recommends. It runs without Isaac Sim and needs RT cores.
World is MuJoCo's word for one independent copy of the scene in a batch. Isaac Lab calls the same thing an environment.
Domain randomisation is a training method that varies the simulator's rendering and physics so widely that the real scene falls inside the range the policy has seen.
aarch64 is the 64-bit Arm processor architecture. AWS Graviton and the NVIDIA DGX Spark use it.
A policy is the trained model that reads what the robot observes, here camera images and joint angles, and decides what the motors do next.
Newton is a GPU physics engine built on Warp, and Isaac Lab 3.0 can run its tasks on it. A headless Newton run needs no RTX hardware.
MuJoCo Warp is the GPU version of the MuJoCo physics engine, written in Warp. It steps thousands of worlds at once and includes a batch ray tracer for cameras.
OptiX is NVIDIA's ray-tracing library for RTX GPUs. MuJoCo Warp's optional hardware back end is built on it, and MuJoCo Warp falls back to the Warp back end when OptiX is unavailable.
Training frames per second is the throughput figure in Isaac Lab's benchmark. It counts the simulated frames that a training run processes per second, including the time spent updating the policy.
The USD-Camera is the highest-fidelity camera type in the Isaac Lab paper. It runs out of memory beyond 48 cameras on a 96 GB card.
TiledCamera is Isaac Lab's camera sensor class that draws the camera of every environment in one tiled pass. It scales to several thousand environments.
RayCasterCamera is Isaac Lab's camera that casts its rays with Warp. The Isaac Lab paper found it faster than the tiled camera at low resolutions.
MuJoCo is DeepMind's open-source physics simulator. Its built-in renderers use rasterisation and need no RT cores.
MuJoCo Playground is DeepMind's set of ready-made robot tasks for MuJoCo. It includes the SO-101 pick-cube task, which renders a 64x64 image from the wrist camera.
PhysX is the physics engine inside Isaac Sim. Isaac Lab 3.0 can run its tasks on PhysX or on Newton.
The learner is the component of a training process that updates the policy. Isaac Lab's memory figures include it.
An On-Demand Capacity Reservation is an EC2 reservation type that covers G instances, which Capacity Blocks do not.
A Capacity Block for ML reserves a block of EC2 GPU instances for a fixed period. As of November 2026, the list of supported types holds P and Trainium types and no G type.
